patient.chief_complaint: Visual disturbance, confusion, and severe headache during exercise — first episode 4 weeks ago
patient.hpi:
A 27-year-old British man was referred to the neurology outpatient clinic following an alarming episode 4 weeks ago. He was running during a half-marathon event when, at approximately the 15-kilometre mark, he noticed a flickering haze appear in his right peripheral vision that expanded over approximately 20 minutes into a typical zigzag shimmering arc. He slowed to a walk. During the aura, he also felt confused and disoriented — he didn't recognise other runners around him and couldn't recall his race number momentarily. A St John Ambulance volunteer was called. The visual aura and confusion resolved within 30-35 minutes. He was assessed briefly at the event and was found alert and oriented at that time. Approximately 20 minutes later, he developed a severe bilateral throbbing headache (9/10) with nausea and intense photophobia that lasted approximately 14 hours. He was taken to A&E where he was given IV fluids for dehydration.

He had never had a visual aura before and no prior significant headaches. He completed a head CT in A&E which was reported as normal. He is an active marathon runner (training 50-60 km/week). He is healthy, takes no medications, has no medical history, and no family history of epilepsy. His older sister has migraines without aura. He consumes caffeine strategically around training and does not drink alcohol. He specifically denies any weakness, speech difficulty, or loss of consciousness during or after the episode. He is extremely anxious about exercising again.

family_history: Sister has migraine without aura; no family history of epilepsy, stroke, hemiplegic migraine, or cardiac disease

social_history.note: Sports therapist; competitive marathon runner (50-60 km/week training); non-smoker; no alcohol; high caffeine around races; no illicit drugs

physical_exam.general: Athletic well-appearing man; alert and fully oriented; bradycardic (athlete's heart); no acute distress

differential.key_features: Normal Holter with exercise; no arrhythmia detected; no WPW; sinus bradycardia at rest is physiological for athlete

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Exercise-Triggered Migraine Aura and Confusional Migraine

KEY FINDINGS:
1. EXERCISE-TRIGGERED MIGRAINE: Aerobic exercise can trigger migraine via multiple mechanisms: dehydration/hypoglycaemia, hyperventilation, adenosine release, CSD susceptibility during metabolic stress
2. CONFUSIONAL MIGRAINE (ALICE IN WONDERLAND SYNDROME): ICHD-3 recognises 'migraine with confusional aura' — transient confusion/amnesia as aura; more common in adolescents and young adults; usually resolves within 30-60 min
3. CSD DURING EXERCISE: Intense endurance exercise reduces cortical threshold for CSD, particularly with dehydration and glycogen depletion
4. MARATHON CONTEXT: Dehydration, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia at 15 km in a half-marathon are all CSD triggers converging
5. DIFFERENTIAL: Exercise-induced hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, or posterior cortex hypoperfusion during maximal exertion — all must be considered
6. PROGNOSIS: Most exercise-triggered migraine resolves spontaneously; preventive during race season may be considered

CONCLUSION: Exercise-triggered migraine with visual and confusional aura. Address dehydration, glycogen loading, and race-day caffeine management.
output.summary: Exercise-triggered migraine with confusional aura (CSD during metabolic stress of marathon); dehydration + glycogen depletion + hyperventilation all lower CSD threshold

output.rhythm_summary: Normal Holter with exercise; no arrhythmia; athlete's sinus bradycardia at rest; no WPW
output.impression: Normal Holter with exercise; no arrhythmia; athlete's sinus bradycardia at rest; no WPW

findings:
TRANSTHORACIC ECHOCARDIOGRAM

Findings: Athletic LVH pattern — borderline increased wall thickness (IVSd 11mm, normal <12mm in athletes). Normal systolic function, EF 64%. Normal valves.

BUBBLE STUDY: Small PFO detected — 3-4 microbubbles crossing during Valsalva. No spontaneous shunt at rest.

NOTE: PFO prevalence ~25% in general population; higher frequency reported in migraineurs. PFO closure NOT indicated for exercise-triggered migraine without prior confirmed stroke (PREMIUM/MIST trials).

IMPRESSION: Athletic LVH pattern. Small incidental PFO — no action needed.
output.impression: Athletic LVH (physiological); small PFO — incidental; PFO closure not indicated for migraine alone

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Migraine Prevention in Endurance Athletes

KEY FINDINGS:
1. HYDRATION: Most critical intervention; target pre-race weight maintenance with electrolyte sports drink; prevent >2% body weight loss
2. CARBOHYDRATE LOADING: 7-10 g/kg/day CHO for 3 days pre-race; prevents glycogen depletion-triggered CSD at high-effort threshold
3. CAFFEINE TIMING: Withdrawal headache if regular caffeine is stopped before race; alternatively consistent daily intake reduces withdrawal risk; excessive acute caffeine (energy gels) during a race can trigger migraine in some individuals
4. PREVENTIVE MEDICATIONS: Beta-blockers (propranolol) REDUCE exercise tolerance — avoid in competitive athletes. Topiramate 25-50 mg/day does not impair exercise; amitriptyline may cause fatigue; anti-CGRP antibodies show no exercise limitation
5. TRIPTAN: Take at headache ONSET; not during aura; naratriptan has longer t½ and may be useful for predictable race-day migraines (taken pre-race — limited evidence)

CONCLUSION: Optimise hydration/carbohydrate loading; avoid propranolol (reduces exercise tolerance); topiramate or anti-CGRP preventive options for athlete.
output.summary: Hydration + carbohydrate loading key for exercise-triggered migraine; avoid beta-blockers in competitive athletes (reduce exercise tolerance); topiramate or CGRP antibodies are athlete-compatible preventives

output.report:
LITERATURE SEARCH: PRES vs Exertional Migraine — Differential Diagnosis

KEY FINDINGS:
1. POSTERIOR REVERSIBLE ENCEPHALOPATHY SYNDROME (PRES): Typically associated with hypertensive emergency, immunosuppressive agents (ciclosporin, tacrolimus), eclampsia; MRI shows posterior white matter T2/FLAIR signal change — NOT present in this patient
2. EXERTION-INDUCED HYPERTENSION: Extreme exercise can transiently raise BP to 180+/100+ during maximal effort; transient hypertension could theoretically cause PRES in susceptible individuals; however, this patient has no history of hypertension and normal resting BP
3. MRI FINDING: Normal MRI in this case — no posterior FLAIR change; excludes PRES
4. EXERTIONAL HEADACHE: Primary exertional headache (ICHD-3 4.2) is bilateral, without aura; this patient has unilateral aura + confusion — more consistent with exercise-triggered migraine with aura

CONCLUSION: PRES excluded by normal MRI. Exercise-triggered migraine with confusional aura is the diagnosis.
output.summary: PRES excluded by normal MRI (no posterior FLAIR signal change); exercise-triggered migraine with confusional aura confirmed
